transcript.name: Wei Zhou
transcript.text: I'm concerned we might miss something if we try to settle this too quickly. Maybe we should look at recent feedback—see what actually worked for our clients and where we slipped up.

transcript.name: Rafael Carvalho
transcript.text: I like Wei’s idea. Let’s take ten minutes, pull up the last client feedback—good and bad. No overthinking, just the main themes. Then we use that as the backbone for our pitch. Fair?

transcript.name: Trang Nguyen
transcript.text: Do we have the most recent client feedback on hand? I can open up the shared folder if that's easier.

transcript.name: Erik Lundström
transcript.text: Makes sense to me. Looking at feedback keeps things focused. How recent are those files, Trang?

transcript.name: Lilian Njoroge
transcript.text: Pulling up the latest feedback’s a good idea. But let’s make sure we don’t gloss over any big patterns—sometimes little complaints add up.

transcript.name: Todd Ramsey
transcript.text: I’m good with scanning the feedback, but let’s watch out for getting stuck on the outliers. Patterns matter more than the odd complaint.

transcript.name: Helena Baxter
transcript.text: Enough. Trang, open the feedback folder. Rafael, you and Wei skim for patterns. I want three bullet points that set us apart—ten minutes, tops. We pick a lead after. No more circling.

transcript.name: Lucía Mendoza
transcript.text: Okay, so once Rafael and Wei have those points from the feedback, do we want to talk through who feels comfortable leading the pitch? I just want to make sure we’re clear before we move on.

transcript.name: Élise Moreau
transcript.text: I think looking at the feedback is smart. Can we make sure we cover both what we did well and where clients thought we missed the mark? Sometimes the less obvious stuff is what trips us up.

transcript.name: Amitesh Iyer
transcript.text: If we're looking for themes, maybe someone can call them out as you spot them? I can help jot down points if that's useful. Just let me know.

transcript.name: Trang Nguyen
transcript.text: Folder’s open now—let me know if you have trouble finding anything. Rafael, Wei, it’s all yours.

transcript.name: Wei Zhou
transcript.text: Maybe as we read through, if something jumps out, just say it out loud. That way we don't miss a point and can spot patterns faster.

transcript.name: Élise Moreau
transcript.text: If people start spotting themes, maybe we should take a pause every few minutes. Just to make sure everyone’s had a chance to speak up or add something we might’ve missed.

transcript.name: Lucía Mendoza
transcript.text: If anyone’s worried about missing a point, just say it out loud—even if it feels small. I’ll keep a list too, just in case. That way, nobody’s left out.

transcript.name: Helena Baxter
transcript.text: Enough with the lists and pauses. Rafael and Wei, call out patterns as you see them. Amitesh, jot them down. We don’t need a group hug—just results. Ten minutes, then we pick a lead. That’s it.

transcript.name: Erik Lundström
transcript.text: Alright, I’ll listen in for anything that jumps out. If something feels off or repeats, I’ll call it out. Let’s try to keep it moving.

transcript.name: Todd Ramsey
transcript.text: Heard. I’ll listen for repeats or anything odd as you go.

transcript.name: Rafael Carvalho
transcript.text: Alright, jumping in—first thing I’m seeing from feedback: clients liked how responsive we were when things changed last minute. That comes up a lot. Anyone else spot something?

transcript.name: Lucía Mendoza
transcript.text: Being quick to adapt is great. Has anyone seen feedback on what tripped us up, too? Just so we cover both sides.

transcript.name: Erik Lundström
transcript.text: I keep seeing that being flexible is a plus for us. But if there’s a snag that keeps repeating, we should probably call that out, too. Anyone notice a pattern on the downside?

transcript.name: Amitesh Iyer
transcript.text: One thing I’ve seen pop up—some clients said handovers between our teams got messy, especially when timelines shifted. Maybe that’s something we should own up to?

transcript.name: Helena Baxter
transcript.text: Handovers have been sloppy—no point sugarcoating it. We own that in the pitch and say what we’re fixing. That’s how we show we’re not blind to our own gaps.

transcript.name: Todd Ramsey
transcript.text: Yeah, no use pretending handovers weren't a problem. If we’re putting that out front, let’s be specific about what’s changing—not just ‘we’ll do better.’ People want details.

transcript.name: Élise Moreau
transcript.text: If we’re naming the handover problem, maybe we should mention one thing we’ve changed already—like that new checklist, or the buddy system between teams. Just so it’s concrete.

transcript.name: Wei Zhou
transcript.text: We could point to the new handover checklist. It’s not perfect yet, but at least we can show we’re trying something concrete.

transcript.name: Trang Nguyen
transcript.text: Yeah, the checklist helps. Should we also check if anything else keeps popping up in the feedback? Just to be sure we catch all the big stuff.

transcript.name: Rafael Carvalho
transcript.text: Let’s make it concrete. We call out the handover mess, show we’ve started fixing it—checklist, maybe pairing folks from both sides. If anyone thinks that’s not enough, now’s the time to say it.
